words.d: a basic enemy type defined by its behaviour, like a chaser or a shooter
a visible or audible warning before an attack, so the player can react
when an enemy appears in the world
a big, special enemy that blocks progress and tests what the player has learned
a repeating set of moves a boss uses, which players can learn
the place where a boss fight happens

lessons.title: Decide what an enemy does before how it looks

cards.text: The golden rule again: **form follows function.** Decide what an enemy **does** before anyone draws it. Code, animation and art all depend on that decision.

Define seven things first:
- size and behaviour
- speed and movement style
- attacks
- aggression
- health
Together with the level's theme, they tell you who the enemies are and how they work together.
An artist sculpts beautiful wings on a monster, then the design says it burrows underground. Wings wasted, team frustrated. Redoing enemies again and again kills morale.
In tower defense and survivor-likes, an enemy is a row in a spreadsheet: health, speed, armour, target rule, special trait. Write that row before any concept art.
Claws come last.

check.q: What should you define before drawing an enemy?
options: Its behaviour, size, speed, attacks and health
Its colour palette and the style of its outfit
Its name, its lore and its family history
check.why: Function decides form. The art should serve what the enemy does.

cards.text: An enemy's size decides **how you fight it, how much damage it takes, how it reacts to hits** and how proud you feel beating it.
Size tiers: short, average, large, huge and gigantic. Small enemies fly back when hit. Giant ones barely notice. Huge enemies often need special tactics, like hitting a weak spot.
On small screens, size tiers must jump clearly: small fodder, bigger elites, a huge boss. Players should know the threat level at a glance.
Hit a gnome, he flies. Hit a giant, he yawns.

check.q: How should a giant enemy usually react to a normal hit?
options: Barely react at all
Fly across the screen
Die instantly
check.why: Size sets the reaction. Big enemies shrug off small hits.

cards.text: Behaviour is the soul of an enemy. **Don't repeat behaviours. Combine ones that complement each other**, so groups of enemies become combat puzzles.

Ten classic behaviours:
- **patroller**, **chaser**, **shooter**, **guard**
- **flyer**, **bomber**, **burrower**
- **teleporter**, **blocker**, and a **doppelganger** that copies you
A shooter hiding behind a blocker forces the player to think: break the shield first, or go around? Mixed behaviours make players do quick threat analysis.
Survivor-likes rely on this: chasers swarm you, shooters keep their distance, bombers punish standing still. Each wave mixes them so every run feels different.

check.q: Why combine different enemy behaviours in one fight?
options: It turns the fight into a puzzle
It's cheaper to build each enemy
It makes every enemy weaker
check.why: Complementary behaviours force players to think about which threat to handle first.

lessons.title: Speed, size and strength trade off

cards.text: Speed makes enemies scarier and harder to hit. But **speed, size and strength trade off.** An enemy with all three feels cheap.
How an enemy moves defines its personality too. Aim between random and predictable. Borrow from nature: crabs move sideways, wolves circle, bugs zigzag.
In many action games, henchmen attack one at a time while the others wait. It looks a bit silly up close, but it keeps fights fair and readable.
Fast enemies need very clear tells on mobile, because touch reactions are slower than buttons. If a fast enemy is also tough, give it a clear weak spot.
Small and speedy, or big and beefy. Never both, or it's cheesy.

check.q: An enemy is huge, very fast and very strong. What's the problem?
options: It feels cheap and unfair
Nothing: it's a great challenge
It's too easy
check.why: Each strength should come with a weakness. All three at once feels unfair.

lessons.title: How enemies think and get around

cards.text: Sit down with your programmer and decide **how enemies move around the level and how they think.** **Waypoints**, set points they travel between, are the usual tool.
Five questions: Can it move around? Is it aggressive? Does it work with other enemies? Does it defend something? Can it adapt to different situations?
In tower defense, enemy paths are the level design. Players place towers along the path, so the route must be clear, readable and fair.
My Angry Troops Defend Valiantly: Mobile, Aggressive, Team player, Defensive, Versatile.

options: Set points an enemy moves between
Health pickups placed along a path
Save points the player can return to
check.why: Waypoints give enemies a planned route through the level.

cards.text: How an enemy **enters** and **leaves** matters as much as how it fights. A great entrance says "new, exciting, dangerous!" A fair spawn and a juicy death make fighting fun.
Introduce each new enemy with a moment: it bursts from the ground, crashes through a wall, or stands in a spotlight. Never spawn enemies right behind the player where they can't be seen.
A skeleton that just stands there is a mannequin. A skeleton that explodes out of its grave is a memory.
Show a "new enemy" card the first time players meet one: its name and a one-line tip on how to beat it. And make deaths fade fast, so cheap phones don't lag.
Entrances are trailers; deaths are confetti.

options: Right behind the player, out of sight
In front of the player, in clear view
From a doorway the player can see
check.why: Hidden spawns cause unfair hits. Players should see threats arrive.

cards.text: If players **avoid** an enemy because it's too hard, too cheap or too annoying, the design failed. **Give players reasons to want the fight.**

Six reasons to fight:
- **loot:** it drops rewards
- **path:** it blocks the way
- **key:** it carries something you need
- **power:** beating it makes you stronger
- **taunts:** it makes you angry
- **looking badass:** the fight is just cool
An enemy that drops nothing, blocks nothing and takes forever to kill will be skipped every time.
In F2P, rewards and progress drive most fights. Make sure every enemy type drops something or moves the player forward.
Loot, Path, Key, Power, Taunts, Badass.

check.q: Players keep running past an enemy. What's the likely problem?
options: There's no good reason to fight it
It's too hard, so players avoid it
It's too small for players to notice
check.why: Without loot, progress or fun, fighting isn't worth the risk.

cards.text: Let enemies have cool, varied attacks. But **every attack must be telegraphed** with a readable warning, so observant players can respond.
A tell can be a wind-up animation, a glow, a sound, a flash, or a marker on the ground. Players learn the tell, then react. That's what makes them feel skilful.
An attack with no warning isn't hard. It's a coin flip, and players hate losing to luck.
On mobile, every damaging attack needs a wind-up plus a ground marker or aim line that stays visible under the thumb. Players glance at small screens quickly.
No tell, no hell.

check.q: Why must enemy attacks be telegraphed?
options: So players can learn and react
To make the enemies weaker
To show off the animation work
check.why: Without warnings, success is luck, not skill.

lessons.title: Annoy without damage, and balance health

cards.text: Not every enemy attack has to take health. **"Grief" attacks** disrupt, delay or annoy instead, adding variety. And every enemy must be killable, with health balanced against the player's attacks.
Ten grief tools: block, knock back, stun, freeze, heal other enemies, buff other enemies, steal, drain, surprise, and make the player vulnerable.
A thief enemy that grabs your coins and runs is more memorable than one that just hits you. You chase it with real anger.
Match-3 blockers are grief tools: ice that blocks a tile, chocolate that spreads, a bomb that counts down. They create tension without a health bar.

check.q: Which is a "grief" attack, not damage?
options: Stealing the player's coins
A heavy sword hit
A fireball from far away
check.why: Grief attacks disrupt the player without simply draining health.

cards.text: In games, **anything can be an enemy.** Pick from the classics, or invent foes from your theme and story. Tie them together visually, reuse smartly, and make sure they belong in your world.
Reusing an enemy with a new colour is fine, if it keeps the same behaviour. **If the behaviour changes, the look must change too.** Otherwise players are tricked.
A red ninja and a blue ninja that fight the same way: fine. A blue ninja that suddenly throws bombs while looking like the red one: unfair.
Live games add new enemy variants every season. Keep a clear visual rule, like elites always glow, so players read new variants instantly.
Same ninja, new paint, new trick? Never.

check.q: You reuse an enemy model but give it new attacks. What must change?
options: Its look, so players notice the difference
Nothing: players learn the new attacks
Only its name in the enemy list
check.why: New behaviour needs a new look, or players feel tricked.

lessons.title: Make the player hate the villain

cards.text: Introduce your main villain memorably, and **make the player hate them** in ways that hurt the player's gameplay. Keep the villain alive to return.
The best villains take something from the player: steal a power, kidnap a helper, destroy the base. Taunts and idle animations make them seem smart and alive. Sometimes, let the villain win a round.
A villain who kidnaps the character who heals you is hated far more than one who only gives speeches. It hits your gameplay, not just the story.
In LiveOps, a recurring villain can run across a whole event, with a final fight at the end, and return next season. Players love a rival who keeps coming back.
Steal the healer, not just the heart.

check.q: What makes players truly hate a villain?
options: It takes something the player uses in play
It gives a long, evil speech
It has a scary name and a dark cape
check.why: Losing something you rely on makes the anger personal.

cards.text: You can push and punish players without anything to fight. Four "enemies" that aren't monsters: **gremlins, tormentors, time and other humans.**

- **Gremlin:** something that messes with you, like a creature stealing items.
- **Tormentor:** an unbeatable threat you must escape.
- **Time:** a countdown.
- **Humans:** real opponents, or even the friend next to you on the couch.
Time is the most common enemy in mobile games: move limits, event countdowns and timed bonus rounds create pressure with no monster at all.

check.q: Which "non-enemy enemy" is most common in mobile games?
options: Time: countdowns and move limits
Dragons guarding treasure
Ghosts that haunt the board
check.why: Timers and limited moves create pressure without any monster.

cards.text: A boss is not just a big monster with lots of health. **It's a carefully built machine that tests what the player has learned**, and it must be built on a **finished** player moveset.

Choose one approach: **test** moves the player already knows, **or** teach a new ability and then test it. Don't do both at full strength. Also ask what the boss **means**: what it wants, what it represents, what fans expect.
Three kinds of boss: physical (muscle), mental (a puzzle or trick), and global (a disaster or huge threat).
In puzzle games, chapter-end "Hard" and "Super Hard" levels are the bosses. They block progress and end a chapter with a climax.
Boss = blocker + climax.

check.q: Why build a boss only after the player's moves are finished?
options: The boss tests those moves
Bosses are cheap to rebuild
Players often skip bosses
check.why: If the player's moves change, the boss fight breaks.

cards.text: Build the boss fight from **learnable patterns** with four parts, and make it escalate like a dance. **Always let the player land the final blow.**

- **Primary attack:** its main move.
- **Invulnerable attack:** a move you must avoid, not fight.
- **Vulnerable state:** a moment it's open to damage.
- **Opportunity:** what the player does in that moment.
Each round, the pattern gets faster or adds a move.
Big bosses cause camera headaches: keep the boss and the player both in view. And never let the boss die from a cutscene or a random hit. The player swings last.
On mobile, pin the boss health bar at the top with phase markers. Make weak points glow, and make vulnerable windows obvious.
PIVO: Primary, Invulnerable, Vulnerable, Opportunity. The player swings last. Always.

check.q: Who should land the final blow in a boss fight?
options: The player
A cutscene
An ally character
check.why: The win must feel earned. Taking the last hit away steals the reward.

lessons.title: The arena is half the boss

cards.text: Where a boss fight happens is as important as the fight. **The arena is part of the battle**, and sometimes the level itself is the boss.
Use the arena: platforms that collapse, pillars to hide behind, hazards the boss can be tricked into. Changing the arena between phases keeps a long fight fresh.
Repeated weekly bosses get stale. Changing arena elements each week keeps the same boss interesting without building a new one.
Real estate is half the boss.

check.q: How can you keep a long boss fight fresh?
options: Change the arena between phases
Give the boss much more health
Make the boss move more slowly
check.why: A changing arena gives new challenges without a new boss.

cards.text: Bosses have real downsides: they're expensive, they can break pacing, and they can become walls that stop players. One fix: **replace a big creature with big drama.**
A personal, story-driven confrontation can hit harder than a giant monster: a tense standoff, a betrayal, a choice under pressure.
A dagger an inch from your eye is scarier than a robot the size of Tokyo.
Watch the fail rate and quitting on every boss level. Soften true walls, and offer a fair free path, like an earned booster or an ad. Never make a boss beatable only by paying.
Drama beats scale.

check.q: What's a risk of a very hard boss in F2P?
options: Players hit a wall and quit
Players spend less time
Nothing
check.why: Skill walls cause churn. Watch fail rates and keep a fair path forward.

cards.text: Bosses are a favourite **LiveOps event** format. They bring players together, create a shared goal, and give a big climax.

- **Clan boss:** a giant boss your whole clan hits over days. Rewards grow with total damage.
- **Raid boss:** appears for a limited time, and players group up (Pokémon GO raids).
- **Weekly boss:** repeatable, with capped rewards (Genshin Impact).

Readability checklist:
- a clear silhouette for each enemy type
- size tiers that jump clearly
- a glow for elite enemies
- a warning for every attack
- a "new enemy" card on first meeting
Tension is fine. **Engineered** failure, hidden odds, or a boss that only payers can beat is not. Celebrate the win after a hard boss level more than anything else in the chapter.

check.q: What makes a clan boss event engaging?
options: A shared goal the whole clan works on
Each player fights the boss alone
Only paying players can take part
check.why: Shared goals create teamwork and social obligation.
